items.prose: Four forecasts of a daily return are 0.3, −0.2, 0.1 and 0.4 (%). What happened was 0.1, −0.5, 0.2 and 0.6.
items.question: What is the mean squared error, in %²?

feedback.correct: Errors 0.2, 0.3, −0.1 and −0.2: squares sum to 0.18, over 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Square each error, then average.

byKey.sum: You added the squares and did not divide by 4.
byKey.hit: That is the hit rate: all four signs agree, though the misses are large.

explain.text: The squares are 0.04, 0.09, 0.01 and 0.04, which sum to 0.18. Over four days that is 0.045. Every sign was right, so the hit rate says 100%.

items.prose: The label is tomorrow's return and you decide at the close of day $t$.
items.question: Select all that apply. Which features leak?

options.text: The closing price at the end of tomorrow's session
A z-score of today's return using this year's mean and sd
A ten-day average that ends tomorrow
Yesterday's return, which was known long before I decide
options.why: It is known well before the decision.

options.text: Today's volume over its trailing 20-day average, ending today
options.why: Both parts are known at the close.

feedback.correct: Tomorrow's close, the year-wide z-score and the average that ends tomorrow.
feedback.generic: Not quite. A feature leaks when it needs something after the close of day $t$.

byKey.yret: Yesterday's return is known before the decision.
byKey.volrel: A trailing average ending today is known at the close.

explain.text: Anything built from tomorrow, or from statistics over days not yet seen, leaks. Trailing windows ending today do not.

items.prose: A spread follows an AR(1) with $\varphi = 0.65$ and innovation variance 1. The forecast is yesterday's value.
items.question: What is its expected squared error?

byKey.mean: That is the long-run mean's error.
byKey.ar1: That is the AR(1) error. Yesterday's value pays more.

explain.text: Yesterday's value misses by a pull to the mean plus fresh noise: $0.35^2 \times 1.7316 + 1 = 1.2121$.

items.prose: On the same test rows, a rental baseline has RMSE 62.4 and the model has 24.9.
items.question: By what percentage does the model cut the RMSE?

feedback.generic: Not quite. One minus the ratio of the two RMSEs.

byKey.diff: You gave the difference in RMSE, not a percentage.

explain.text: The model's RMSE is 39.9% of the baseline's, so the cut is 60.1%.

items.prose: Daily returns are independent with a standard deviation of 0.8%.
items.question: What is the ten-day standard deviation, in %?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply by the square root of ten.

byKey.linear: You multiplied by 10. Variances add, not standard deviations.

explain.text: Ten independent days have ten times the variance, so the spread is $0.8\sqrt{10} = 2.530$%.

items.prose: Returns on days 1 to 6 are 0.6, −0.3, 0.5, 0.2, 0.7 and −0.4 (%). A four-day rolling mean is shifted by one day.
items.question: What is the shifted mean held on day 6?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Day 6 holds the mean that ended on day 5.

byKey.unshifted: You averaged days 3 to 6. That uses day 6's own return.

explain.text: The mean of days 2 to 5 is $(-0.3 + 0.5 + 0.2 + 0.7)/4 = 0.275$. The unshifted mean on day 6 would be 0.25.

items.prose: Two features correlate 0.75. The variance inflation of the pair is $1/(1 - 0.5625) = 2.2857$.
items.question: By what factor are their standard errors inflated?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Standard errors grow by the root of the variance inflation.

byKey.vif: That is the variance inflation. Take its root.

explain.text: Variances inflate by 2.2857, so standard errors inflate by its square root, 1.5119.

items.prose: A model of tomorrow's close on today's close, on a different index future, reports R² = 0.981.
items.question: What does that show?

options.text: Only that prices persist, so it says nothing of skill
That the model correctly predicts 98% of tomorrow's price
options.why: You read R² as skill. A price level carries its own past.

options.text: That it beats a model of the return
options.why: The return model scores far lower because returns hardly persist, not because it is worse.

options.text: That the close price leaks tomorrow's price to the model
options.why: No leak is needed. Any slow series scores like this.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what copying yesterday would score.

byKey.beats: You compared a level with a return.
byKey.leak: You looked for a leak where none is needed.

explain.text: A price level wanders slowly, so a model that copies yesterday scores nearly as well. Judge against that baseline.

items.question: A forecaster of daily returns is checked on 400 unseen days. Squared errors (× 10⁻⁴): zero forecast 3.10, training mean 3.12, new model 3.19.

parts.question: What is the model's out-of-sample R² against the zero forecast?

feedback.generic: Not quite. One minus the model's error over the zero forecast's.

byKey.flip: You flipped the sign. The model is worse, so R² is negative.
byKey.ratio: You gave the ratio. R² is one minus it.

explain.text: The model's error is 2.9% above the zero forecast's, so R² is −0.029.

parts.question: Does the model beat the best baseline?

options.text: No: the zero forecast is best, with the lower error
Yes: 3.19 is within 3% of 3.10, so it is as good
options.why: Close is not better. A model has to beat the baseline.

options.text: Yes: it is close to the training mean's error of 3.12
options.why: You compared it with a weaker baseline. The best of the three is zero.

options.text: It is a tie, so I would ship the model anyway
options.why: The model has the higher error. There is no tie.

feedback.correct: The zero forecast is best, and the model is worse.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare with the lowest baseline error.

byKey.tie: You called a loss a tie.

explain.text: The best baseline has error 3.10. The model's 3.19 is higher, so it has not beaten it.

parts.question: A rule says the model must cut the best baseline's error by 5%. What error must it reach?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the best baseline's error by 0.95.

byKey.plus: You added 5%. The model must be lower, not higher.

items.prose: A model has a test RMSE of 9.6 with a bootstrap 95% interval of 7.4 to 11.8. The training-mean baseline has an RMSE of 24.0.
items.question: Which sentence is supportable?

options.text: Far better than the baseline, with an error of about ±2.2
The model's error is exactly 9.6, with no uncertainty to report
options.why: You dropped the interval. Test rows leave the figure uncertain.

options.text: The interval reaches 11.8, so the model may not beat the baseline
options.why: Even 11.8 is far below 24.0, so the model clearly beats it.

options.text: The model halves the baseline error, since 9.6 is half of 24

feedback.correct: A clear win, with an uncertainty of about ±2.2.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the interval with the baseline.

byKey.tie: You overlooked that 11.8 is well below 24.0.

explain.text: The whole interval sits far below 24.0, so the win is clear. The interval is about 2.2 either side.
